conclusion: NULL RESULT. T1 was cancelled at its evidence gate, on operator decision. The status is 'failed' only because this record has no latency phases by design. No T1 experiment ran, and none failed. T1's variable was the Python tokenizer code. T0 (run 20261021T102818Z) shows that both gate conditions hold. (1) The tokenizer is not pure Python: it is Hugging Face tokenizers 0.23.2, a Rust core behind PyO3, and Python is about 2% of tokenizer samples. (2) Tokenisation is negligible end to end. On a warm request, fit p50 is 0.83 ms, 0.12% of the handler by mean. On a cold start, Tokenizer.from_file p50 is 0.83 s; it is 0% of REPORT Init Duration and at most 2.3% of the cold first request. Under SnapStart, init runs before the snapshot and is not re-run. On the restored first request, fit is 1.3% of the handler by mean, and tokenizers.so is 0.49% of restore CPU, so the tail is mostly waiting. Any Python-side optimisation could reach at most a fraction of that under-0.2% warm share, so it would fall inside run-to-run spread and be reported as no improvement. The only material cost is the 0.6-0.8 s from_file, which is native serde_json parsing (83% inclusive). That cost is outside T1's variable; it belongs to T2 or T3 if anyone pursues it. Limitations: the gate relies on T0's measurements: Lambda shares from P3 run 20261020T231634Z with cProfile upper bounds, and fixed-host Graviton3 profiles that were repeated on one host on one day. T1 took no measurements of its own. Cost: $0 new AWS spend.
hypothesis: Optimising the existing Python tokenizer code (same algorithm, vocabulary and semantics), profile-led and parity-gated, reduces tokenizer and end-to-end latency. Gated on T0: if the tokenizer is not pure Python or is negligible end to end, the result is null.
